item.title: JPMorgan warns AI-driven stock momentum echoes dot-com era extremes
item.description:
JPMorgan's note points to a market increasingly vulnerable to a sharp reversal, given how concentrated gains have become in a small cluster of AI-linked names. A decoupling between momentum and traditional fundamentals such as valuation and quality suggests investors are chasing price action rather than underlying strength, a pattern that has historically preceded steep drawdowns once momentum trades unwind. Rising volatility in momentum-heavy markets, highlighted by recent swings in Korean memory stocks, adds to the case that positioning has become stretched. The bank's suggestion to rotate toward value and diversify geographically signals growing institutional caution even as headline earnings numbers remain strong, and could foreshadow increased rotation flows out of crowded AI trades in the coming months.

---

Earlier:

  • This may be one of the most important charts in the stock market now

JPMorgan says today's AI-fuelled momentum rally is one of the fastest on record, and is starting to show the same warning signs that preceded past busts.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan says the current momentum-driven rally ranks among the four largest of the last 40 years by size, and second by speed, behind only the 1999 internet boom
  • The bank's systematic research team says correlation between momentum and other factors like valuation and quality is falling, suggesting investors are increasingly just chasing rising prices
  • Rising volatility among popular momentum stocks, including recent swings in Korea's memory chip names, is flagged as another warning sign
  • Warning signs are visible across technology and industrials, and in Japan and emerging market equities
  • JPMorgan recommends investors diversify by style toward value and by geography to guard against losses typically seen once momentum rallies end
  • Separately, the bank says second-quarter S&P 500 earnings growth is tracking near 38% year-on-year, which would mark a second straight quarter of 20%-plus growth, though paper gains from hyperscalers' private AI investments are skewing the figure; stripping those out still leaves growth around 19%, driven largely by capital spending flowing into the semiconductor sector

JPMorgan has warned that the AI-driven rally powering US equity markets is showing early signs of strain, even as the underlying earnings picture for corporate America remains robust.

In a note reviewing market positioning, the bank's strategists said the current bout of momentum-driven investing ranks among the four largest in scale seen over the past 40 years, and is the second fastest on record, trailing only the dot-com era boom of 1999. The comparison underscores how heavily markets have come to rely on a narrow set of AI-linked winners to drive broader index gains.

JPMorgan's systematic research desk flagged a growing disconnect between momentum and other traditional investment factors such as valuation and quality. According to the bank, that gap suggests investors are increasingly buying into rising share prices themselves rather than underlying company fundamentals, a dynamic strategists view as an early warning sign. The bank also pointed to sharply increased volatility among the market's most popular names as further evidence that risk is building, citing recent turbulence in South Korea's memory chip-focused equity market as a case in point.

The bank said these warning signs extend beyond the technology sector into industrials, and are visible geographically in both Japan and emerging markets. Given the tendency for momentum-led rallies to unwind quickly once they turn, JPMorgan is advising investors to diversify their portfolios, both by shifting some exposure toward value style stocks and by broadening geographic allocation, as a hedge against the kind of rapid capital losses that have historically followed similar booms.

On the earnings side, JPMorgan struck a more constructive tone. The bank noted that the second quarter earnings season has been strong, powered primarily by spending tied to artificial intelligence and the energy sector. Consensus estimates point to S&P 500 earnings per share growing by roughly 38% year over year, which would mark a second consecutive quarter of growth above 20%, a rare run by historical standards.

However, JPMorgan cautioned that the headline growth figure is partly inflated by large unrealised gains booked by major hyperscale technology companies on their investments in private AI firms. Stripping out those paper gains, the bank said, underlying earnings growth would still be strong at around 19%. The bank noted that growth remains heavily concentrated, tracking the flow of capital expenditure away from the hyperscalers themselves and into semiconductor companies, which JPMorgan estimates are now responsible for more than half of the index's overall earnings growth.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Oil recap - Oil prices mixed as Hormuz reopening hopes offset surprise US crude build
item.description:
The tug of war between de-escalation hopes in the Strait of Hormuz and a surprise build in US crude stocks looks set to keep oil choppy and directionless in the near term. Any confirmed announcement on an Iran-Oman arrangement, particularly one involving a US-Iran return to talks, would likely trigger a sharper downside move given how much of the war-risk premium is currently priced in. Conversely, continued Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers and disruption to Black Sea and Caspian export routes provide a floor under prices and keep volatility elevated. Traders will be watching Friday as a potential deadline for a Hormuz announcement, with sentiment likely to swing hard on headline risk either way.

---

Oil markets are caught between fading war risk in the Gulf and a surprise inventory build, with a possible Hormuz deal looming as soon as Friday.

Summary:

  • Brent settled up around $79 a barrel while WTI eased to around $75, as markets weighed a possible US-Iran de-escalation deal over the Strait of Hormuz
  • Iran denied peace talks were underway but said it and Oman have reached an understanding on managing the strait, with a joint announcement being finalised
  • Houthi rebels said they attacked a Saudi oil tanker off Yanbu, and separately claimed attacks on tankers in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, vowing to escalate
  • US crude inventories rose by around 2.5 million barrels versus an expected draw of around 1.5 million barrels, pressuring WTI further
  • Disruption continued at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium and in the Black Sea, adding to global supply uncertainty
  • Later reports point to a deal nearing finalisation: the WSJ cited sources saying a US-Iran return to talks could follow, CNN cited a Gulf official putting the odds of a deal by Friday at "50:50," the FT reported an initial arrangement where Iranian ships would clear mines from the waterway before it reopens, and Israeli outlet N12 reported senior US and mediating-country officials saying an announcement could come as early as that night

Oil prices were mixed on Wednesday, with Brent crude edging higher while the US benchmark slipped, as investors weighed revived hopes for a de-escalation between the United States and Iran that could reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and restore oil flows across the Middle East.

Brent crude futures settled up around $79 a barrel, a modest gain on the session, while West Texas Intermediate futures fell to around $75, down circa 0.7%. The moves followed a sharp selloff a day earlier, when reports of progress in ending the conflict drove prices down by around 5%, pulling Brent below $80 for the first time since mid July.

US President Donald Trump described an "all-day negotiation" with Iran on Tuesday in largely positive terms, while also warning Tehran would be hit hard if no deal is reached. Iran's Foreign Ministry pushed back on characterisations of formal peace talks, but confirmed Iran and Oman have reached an understanding on managing the strait, with a joint announcement said to be in its final stages. Before the conflict began at the end of February, roughly a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas moved through the waterway.

Analysts remained cautious on how durable any arrangement might prove. Phil Flynn of Price Futures Group noted that similar agreements in the past have not held for long, while analysts at IG flagged that the key sticking point remains whether Iran retains a degree of control over the strait or whether the US insists on ceding none.

On the supply side, US crude inventories rose by around 2.5 million barrels last week, according to Energy Information Administration data, confounding expectations for a draw of roughly 1.5 million barrels. Inventories at the Cushing, Oklahoma storage hub also climbed more than expected, according to Andrew Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates, adding pressure to the US contract. Diesel stocks posted a surprise draw, lifting diesel futures modestly, while gasoline futures pared earlier losses after a larger than expected drawdown in gasoline stocks.

Losses were capped by renewed shipping risk in the Red Sea, after Yemen's Houthi rebels said they attacked a Saudi oil tanker off the Yanbu export terminal, and separately claimed strikes on tankers in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, vowing to continue and escalate operations against Saudi oil shipping. Disruption also persisted in the Black Sea, where attacks on Russian and Ukrainian ships, ports and terminals continue to hit commodity flows, while the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, the main export route for Kazakh crude, repeatedly suspended loadings this week citing safety concerns and a shortage of tankers. Separately, China further eased restrictions on fuel exports for August.

Later updates suggested momentum toward a deal was building. The Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources, that a confirmed arrangement would see the US and Iran resume talks covering Iran's nuclear programme and financial relief, with Oman and Qatar pushing for incentives such as sanctions waivers on oil. CNN cited a Gulf official putting the odds of a US-Iran deal by Friday at roughly even. The Financial Times reported that under an initial phase, Iran would send vessels, including tankers, through the strait to clear mines before it reopens to wider shipping, with no fees charged during that period, and that a holding deal would see Washington lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and reinstate a waiver allowing Iran to sell oil and related products. Israeli outlet N12, citing its correspondent Ravid, reported that senior US officials and sources in the mediating countries said an agreement to reopen the strait could be announced as early as that evening. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Cook: Fed running out of room for disnflation to return
item.description:
Cook's remarks add to a building chorus of Fed officials flagging openness to tightening, a shift traders will read as hawkish after last week's split decision to hold rates steady. With three dissenting votes already on record favouring a hike, markets may start pricing higher odds of a rate increase at the next meeting, particularly if upcoming inflation prints disappoint. The dollar and short-term yields are the most likely near-term movers on this kind of commentary, while equities could face pressure if the narrative of an increasingly divided, inflation-focused Fed takes hold. Cook's acknowledgment that tariffs, the Middle East conflict and AI-related investment could still ease price pressures leaves room for a less aggressive path, tempering the immediate hawkish read.

---

Cook opens the door to a Fed rate hike, citing dwindling patience with elevated inflation even as she leaves room for prices to cool on their own.

Summary:

  • Fed Governor Lisa Cook says she would support raising rates if inflation does not moderate
  • Cook views inflation risks as outweighing risks to the job market
  • She warns the Fed is running out of room to keep waiting for disinflation
  • Cook was among the majority who voted to hold rates steady last week, a decision that drew three dissents favouring a hike
  • Other officials, including New York Fed's Williams and Philadelphia Fed's Paulson, have also signalled openness to hiking
  • Cook says AI has not yet caused notable job losses and the labour market remains resilient

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said on Wednesday she is prepared to support raising the central bank's benchmark interest rate if inflation does not resume its downward trend, citing mounting risk that elevated prices could become embedded in the economy.

Speaking in prepared remarks to the 2026 Economic Luncheon of the Anchorage Economic Development Corporation, Cook said the risks tied to inflation currently outweigh the risks to the labour market, and that she would back a hike "if it becomes necessary" to restore price stability. She stressed that outcome is not guaranteed, noting inflation may still cool without further tightening.

Cook argued the Fed has limited room left to wait given how long inflation has run above the central bank's 2 percent target. She warned that persistent overshoot risks getting locked into wage and price setting behaviour, a dynamic she said would be far harder to unwind later. Even so, Cook pointed to tariffs, the conflict in the Middle East and heavy investment tied to artificial intelligence as forces that could still ease price pressures without additional rate action.

Her comments follow last week's Federal Open Market Committee decision to hold the federal funds rate in a range of 3.5 to 3.75 percent, a call that drew three dissenting votes from officials who wanted an immediate increase. Cook was among the majority who backed the pause, saying it was appropriate to see how inflation trends evolve before acting further.

She is not alone in flagging a more hawkish stance. New York Fed President John Williams and Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson have both signalled willingness to raise rates if conditions warrant, adding to a more divided tone among policymakers. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, by contrast, has offered little public guidance on the likely path for rates.

Cook also addressed the labour market and consumer sentiment, saying job conditions have held up and that predictions of significant AI driven job losses have not yet materialised, though she cautioned risks remain. She linked the weak mood among consumers partly to persistently high inflation, underscoring the stakes for the Fed as it weighs its next move. 

---

item.title: At the close: Nasdaq sags as Google falls more than 4%
item.description:
The story of the day in US stock markets was a modestly positive open followed by steady selling until the European close and a flatline until the final minutes when it fell an additional 0.3 percentage points.

A main loser on the day was Google, which fell more than 4% and was a big reason the Nasdaq Composite was down 0.9% on the day. Zooming out, there's clearly an element of profit taking at work after two sensational days to start the week.

Google fell after it was announced that AI wizard Demis Hassabis is stepping away from the day-to-day management of Google DeepMind to become Alphabet’s chief scientist and DeepMind chairman. DeepMind CTO Koray Kavukcuoglu will take over daily responsibility for frontier-model research and Gemini development. Longtime Google AI leader Jeff Dean, along with several other senior researchers, is leaving to create a new AI venture called Discovery Loop.

The fear is that these moves are coming after some sort of stumble in AI development at Google.

On the upside, shares of Nvidia had a strong day, climbing 3.8% in the fifth consecutive day of gains. The market is coming to terms with the idea that the hyperscaler AI capex spending spree will continue, and might even have a positive return on investment. The circular funding argument remains but I don't worry too much. Nvidia is backstopping upwards of $250 billion in spending but its margins are 80% so its economic risk on that is only $50 billion, plus it could re-sell the chips.
